paragraphs.text: Loeys-Dietz syndrome-5 is a connective tissue disorder. Its features overlap with Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome. Craniofacial features include hypertelorism, bifid uvula, and cleft palate. Skeletal features include arachnodactyly, joint hyperextensibility, pectus deformity, scoliosis, and clubfoot. Stature can be short or tall (Rienhoff et al., 2013; Kuechler et al., 2015). Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) showed that cardiovascular involvement varies widely. It includes thoracic and abdominal aortic aneurysm and dissection and mitral valve disease, and some mutation carriers have no cardiovascular abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) reported a 9-year-old European American girl born to nonconsanguineous, healthy parents. At birth she had contractures of the right hand, most severe in the third and fourth fingers, and of all toes. She also had a midline facial nevus flammeus and mild hypotonia. Her birth weight was 2.9 kg (5th centile). At 3 months she was evaluated for failure to thrive and delayed gross motor development. At 17 months she weighed 7.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and had the following features: bilateral pes planus, mild pectus excavatum, hyperextensibility of multiple large joints, mild retrognathia, prominent eyes, hypertelorism, blue sclerae, a small metopic ridge, and a bifid uvula with an intact hard palate. She had decreased bulk in all appendicular and axial muscles, strength of 1/5, low tone, diminished reflexes, and markedly reduced subcutaneous fat. At 20 months she stood independently with a positive Gowers sign, and at 24 months she walked with a 'hip waddle.' Neurocognitive development was appropriate for age. Radiographs showed bilateral coxa valga. A quadriceps biopsy at age 7 years showed type 1 fiber predominance with mild, focal type 1 fiber disproportion consistent with disuse, and no dystrophic or inflammatory changes. At age 7 years she weighed 15.5 kg (less than 1st centile) and was 115 cm tall (5th centile). Yearly echocardiograms from 18 months onward showed no cardiac defect. At age 6.5 years the aortic annulus and root dimensions were normal. The authors described the disorder as a syndrome of low muscle mass, growth retardation, and distal arthrogryposis with features overlapping Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, without evidence of vascular disease.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) studied a large Dutch family (family 1) with features overlapping Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome. Seven family members aged 40 to 68 years had aneurysms and dissections, mainly of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Three died from aortic dissection and rupture. Four family members had mitral valve abnormalities ranging from mild prolapse to severe regurgitation that required surgery. Craniofacial abnormalities were subtle: long face, high-arched palate, and retrognathia. Pectus deformity and scoliosis were frequent. Other recurrent findings were velvety skin, varices, and hiatal hernia. Several family members had autoimmune features, including HLA-B27-positive spondyloarthritis, Graves disease, and celiac disease.

paragraphs.text: Bertoli-Avella et al. (2015) also described 10 additional families. In total they reported 43 affected individuals from 11 families. Vascular involvement ranged from no cardiovascular abnormalities at age 64 years to aortic dissection. Type A dissection occurred at a median age of 51 years (range, 40 to 80 years) and type B dissection at a median age of 44.5 years (range, 30 to 57 years). One patient died from dissection of a cerebral aneurysm at age 55 years. No early arterial dissection or dissection at small aortic dimension was observed, and there was no striking aortic or arterial tortuosity. Other cardiovascular features were mitral valve disease, persistent foramen ovale, and atrial or ventricular septal defects. Typical Loeys-Dietz features were common, including hypertelorism (14 patients), bifid uvula (11), cleft palate (5), cervical spine instability, and clubfoot. Other recurrent features were dolichocephaly, high-arched palate, retrognathia, tall stature, joint hypermobility, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, kyphoscoliosis, and inguinal hernia. Early-onset osteoarthritis was reported in only 2 individuals, and no ectopia lentis was found. One patient had short stature and received growth hormone. The authors noted striking intrafamilial and interfamilial variability. Typical Loeys-Dietz features were present in some patients and completely absent in others. Aortic tissue from a dissected aorta showed elastic fiber fragmentation with increased collagen and proteoglycan deposition.

paragraphs.text: Rienhoff et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in a girl with distal arthrogryposis, hypotonia, bifid uvula, low muscle mass, and growth retardation. They found a de novo heterozygous c.1226G-A transition in the TGFB3 gene, resulting in a cys409-to-tyr (C409Y) substitution, and confirmed it by Sanger sequencing. Before exome sequencing, they had found no mutation in TGFB2, TGFBR1, TGFBR2, SMAD3, FBN1, or FBN2.
